rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Bio: Chance Garton is the host and producer of the Innerverse Podcast, where for over a decade he has investigated consciousness, mythology, symbolism, terrain health, and the psychosomatic language of the human body and mind. A biofield tuning practitioner, he uses tuning forks to help clients resolve physical symptoms, break negative patterns, and return to energetic coherence.

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "How a flow state started a show", "body": "Chance explained that his initial goal for the InnerVerse Podcast was to capture the flow state two people reach when conversing about their passions, with the idea that everyone has had an epiphany nobody else has ever had. He described himself as a former trippy festival kid who moved toward linguistics, energy, and mythology symbolism. Asked for his strangest belief, Chance named the idea that everyone is one consciousness experiencing itself through infinite perspectives, and he said he no longer used psychedelics because he liked his life now."}, {"title": "Beliefs, the body, and biofield tuning", "body": "Chance said he saw injury and illness as messages about beliefs in conflict with a person's potential, and he described the root chakra as a conceptual system he linked, in his view, to to-do-list burnout and trouble sleeping. He said he learned biofield tuning from Eileen Day McKusick's books and tuning forks, practicing on friends and listeners before offering it as a service. On whether the forks work through belief or physical sound, Chance called himself a bothist and compared the forks to training wheels."}, {"title": "Coherence, dissonance, and the power of naming", "body": "Chance used the example of metronomes syncing up to argue that coherent sound can bring dissonance into line, and he suggested that tuning to 440 might be less coherent because of the fractional frequencies it produces. He added that coherence can also work in a negative direction, as he said he saw in media messaging. Chance and a host agreed that naming something, such as the placebo effect or pareidolia, can be a way of dismissing it, and Chance said he was still meditating on the power of names."}, {"title": "Astrotheology, priest craft, and a ring world", "body": "Chance said he had lots of reason to think the Bible was not a historical text and preferred to read it as allegory with astrotheology layers. He described a priest class that, in his account, derived stories from constellations and puns, calling the method the green language. Chance also said he had zero belief in what he called the scientific materialist cosmology, offering as a fun speculation that extra lands lie beyond Antarctica with Mars and Venus as their sun and moon."}, {"title": "Gematria, English, and one being in costumes", "body": "Chance said his friend Marty Leeds demonstrated gematria in a way that was not what he called skitzo, and Chance described a septenary cipher in which the word seven sums to 22, echoing the 22 over 7 approximation of pi. He said he leaned toward a divine rather than human origin for such patterns and called English a highly magical language. Chance also offered his view that sky father and earth mother resolve into one being, like the sun, an actor changing roles."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: I had a free-wheeling conversation with Sumo on the Mystical American Patriots Society podcast, covering my path into biofield tuning, astrotheology, and the symbolism hidden in everyday words.
